prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is notebook 2 of part 1 (regression on hourly bike rentals), after exercise 1 of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: checks how the gap between TabICL and HGBT evolves as the training window grows. `LearningCurveDisplay` would keep the oldest rows of each training fold, so the notebook rebuilds a `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48, max_train_size=train_size, test_size=200)` for each size: every window ends right before the gap, and both models are evaluated on the same last 5 test windows at every size. TabICL runs from 100 to 3,200 rows, HGBT (default hyperparameters, too few rows to nest a search) from 100 to 12,800. A commented line lets students with more compute run TabICL up to 12,800 rows. From this notebook on, TabICL uses `n_estimators=1`, justified by exercise 1; the notebook reminds students to check `n_estimators` on their own data first. A warm-up `fit` before the loop keeps one-off costs out of the timings.

Results of the reference run: TabICL keeps a lower mean MAE at every size where both run, although error bars overlap at some sizes. With a few hundred rows the gap is large; HGBT needs 3,200 rows (about 37 bikes per hour) to match TabICL with 400. As the window grows, HGBT keeps improving up to 3,200 rows and the gap narrows, while TabICL improves more slowly after 400 rows and stops improving after 1,600. The explanation is the inductive bias, the kind of relationship a model type favors by construction: trees build step functions from splits on single features, estimated from few rows, while TabICL's prior mixes smooth curves, linear trends, plateaus and tree-like splits and infers from the context which one fits. With more data, the data pins down the relationship and the inductive bias matters less. The notebook announces that data can also be scarce in only part of a table, such as a rare class, covered by the fraud notebooks.

Timings: HGBT's time less than doubles from 800 to 12,800 rows. TabICL's time barely changes up to a few hundred rows, where fixed costs dominate, then grows by about 1.7 each time the window doubles; at 3,200 rows it is about three times slower than HGBT on the same rows and about twice as slow as HGBT on 12,800 rows. TabICL processes the whole context again at every predict. Through TabAPI the network adds a roughly constant cost per call, so exact ratios differ, but the trend holds.

Place in the course: after exercise 1 (`n_estimators`); next comes the notebook on missing values. The inductive bias reappears in TabICL_decision_boundary. Related scikit-learn course material: learning curves (Selecting the Best Model), time series cross-validation (Evaluating Model Performance).
